entries.b3b3ebdce33dcc4e7f96d5c195ec17c9d1d91da8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv99"/><title type="x-ms">Jonah</title> <div sID="gen20292" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20293" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> book of Jonah, though it be placed here in the midst of the prophetical books of scripture, is yet rather a history than a prophecy; one line of prediction there is in it, <hi type="italic">Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown;</hi> the rest of the book is a narrative of the preface to and the consequences of that prediction. In the midst of the obscure prophecies before and after this book, wherein are many things dark and hard to be understood, which are puzzling to the learned, and are <hi type="italic">strong meat for strong men,</hi> comes in this plain and pleasant story, which is entertaining to the weakest, and <hi type="italic">milk for babes.</hi> Probably Jonah was himself the penman of this book, and he, as Moses and other inspired penmen, records his own faults, which is an evidence that in these writings they designed God's glory and not their own. We read of this same Jonah <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2 Kings xiv. 25</reference>, where we find that he was of Gath-hepher in Galilee, a city that belonged to the tribe of Zebulun, in a remote corner of the land of Israel; for the Spirit, which like the wind, <hi type="italic">blows where it listeth,</hi> will as easily find out Jonah in Galilee as Isaiah at Jerusalem. We find also that he was a messenger of mercy to Israel in the reign of Jeroboam the second; for the success of his arms, in the <hi type="italic">restoring of the coast of Israel,</hi> is said to be <hi type="italic">according to the word of the Lord which he spoke by the hand of his servant Jonah the prophet.</hi> Those prophecies were not committed to writing, but this against Nineveh was, chiefly for the sake of the story that depends upon it, and that is recorded chiefly for the sake of Christ, of whom Jonah was a type; it contains also very remarkable instances of human infirmity in Jonah, and of God's mercy both in pardoning repenting sinners, witness Nineveh, and in bearing with repining saints, witness Jonah. <div eID="gen20293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20294" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20295" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A command given to Jonah to preach at Nineveh, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.1-Jonah.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Jonah's disobedience to that command, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. The pursuit and arrest of him for that disobedience by a storm, in which he was asleep, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.4-Jonah.1.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. IV. The discovery of him, and his disobedience, to be the cause of the storm, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.7-Jonah.1.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. V. The casting of him into the sea, for the stilling of the storm, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.11-Jonah.1.16">ver. 11-16</reference>. VI. The miraculous preservation of his life there in the belly of a fish (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.17">ver. 17</reference>), which was his reservation for further services. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv99"/> <div eID="gen20295" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20294" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">A Commission against Nineveh; The Prophet's Disobedience. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 840.)</title> <div sID="gen20296" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me. <hi type="super">3</hi> But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20297" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The honour God put upon Jonah, in giving him a commission to go and prophesy against Nineveh. <hi type="italic">Jonah</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">a dove,</hi> a proper name for all God's prophets, all his people, who ought to be <hi type="italic">harmless as doves,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">mourn as doves</hi> for the sins and calamities of the land. His father's name was <hi type="italic">Amittai—My truth;</hi> for God's prophets should be sons of truth. To him <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord came—to him it was</hi> (so the word signifies), for God's word is a real thing; men's words are but wind, but God's words are substance. He has been before acquainted with the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord,</hi> and knew his voice from that of a stranger; the orders now given him were, <hi type="italic">Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.2">v. 2</reference>. Nineveh was at this time the metropolis of the Assyrian monarchy, an eminent city (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.11">Gen. x. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">a great city, that great city,</hi> forty-eight miles in compass (some make it much more), great in the number of the inhabitants, as appears by the multitude of infants in it (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.11">ch. iv. 11</reference>), great in wealth (there was no end of its store, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.9">Nah. ii. 9</reference>), great in power and dominion; it was the city that for some time <hi type="italic">ruled over the kings of the earth.</hi> But great cities, as well as great men, are under God's government and judgment. Nineveh was a great city, and yet a heathen city, without the knowledge and worship of the true God. How many great cities and great nations are there that <hi type="italic">sit in darkness</hi> and <hi type="italic">in the valley of the shadow of death!</hi> This great city was a wicked city: <hi type="italic">Their wickedness has come up before me</hi> (their <hi type="italic">malice,</hi> so some read it); <hi type="italic">their wickedness was presumptuous,</hi> and they sinned with <hi type="italic">a high hand.</hi> It is sad to think what a great deal of sin is committed in great cities, where there are many sinners, who are not only all sinners, but making one another sin. <hi type="italic">Their wickedness has come up,</hi> that is, it has come to a high degree, to the highest pitch; the <hi type="italic">measure of it</hi> is <hi type="italic">full</hi> to the brim; <hi type="italic">their wickedness has come up,</hi> as that of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.20-Gen.18.21">Gen. xviii. 20, 21</reference>. It has come up <hi type="italic">before me—to my face</hi> (so the word is); it is a bold and open affront to God; it is sinning against him, <hi type="italic">in his sight;</hi> therefore Jonah must <hi type="italic">cry against it;</hi> he must witness against their great wickedness, and must warn them of the destruction that was coming upon them for it. God is coming forth against it, and he sends Jonah before, to proclaim war, and to sound an alarm. <hi type="italic">Cry aloud, spare not.</hi> He must not whisper his message in a corner, but publish it in the streets of Nineveh; <hi type="italic">he that hath ears let him hear</hi> what God has to say by his prophet against that wicked city. When the cry of sin comes up to God the cry of vengeance comes out against the sinner. He must <hi type="italic">go to Nineveh,</hi> and cry there upon the spot against the wickedness of it. Other prophets were ordered to send messages to the neighbouring nations, and the prophecy of Nahum is particularly <hi type="italic">the burden of Nineveh;</hi> but Jonah must go and carry the message himself: "<hi type="italic">Arise</hi> quickly; apply thyself to the business with speed and courage, and the resolution that becomes a prophet; <hi type="italic">arise, and go to Nineveh.</hi>" Those that go on God's errands must rise and go, must stir themselves to the work cut out for them. The prophets were sent first to the <hi type="italic">lost sheep of the house of Israel,</hi> yet not to them only; they had the children's bread, but Nineveh eats of the crumbs. 2. The dishonour Jonah did to God in refusing to obey his orders, and to go on the errand on which he was sent (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">But Jonah,</hi> instead of rising to go to Nineveh, <hi type="italic">rose up to flee to Tarshish,</hi> to <hi type="italic">the sea,</hi> not bound for any port, but desirous to get away <hi type="italic">from the presence of the Lord;</hi> and, if he might but do that, he cared not whither he went, not as if he thought he could go any where from under the eye of God's inspection, but from his special presence, from the spirit of prophecy, which, when it put him upon this work, he thought himself haunted with, and coveted to get out of the hearing of. Some think Jonah went upon the opinion of some of the Jews that the spirit of prophecy was confined to the land of Israel (which in Ezekiel and Daniel was effectually proved to be a mistake), and therefore he hoped he should get clear of it if he could but get out of the borders of that land. (1.) Jonah would not go to Nineveh to cry against it either because it was a long and dangerous journey thither, and in a road he knew not, or because he was afraid it would be as much as his life was worth to deliver such an ungrateful message to that great and potent city. He <hi type="italic">consulted with flesh and blood,</hi> and declined the embassy because he could not go with safety, or because he was jealous for the prerogatives of his country, and not willing that any other nation should share in the honour of divine revelation; he feared it would be the beginning of the removal of the kingdom of God from the Jews to another nation, that would bring forth more of the fruits of it. He owns himself (<reference osisRef="Jonah.4.2">ch. iv. 2</reference>) that the reason of his aversion to this journey was because he foresaw that the Ninevites would repent, and God would forgive them and take them into favour, which would be a slur upon the people of Israel, who had been so long a peculiar people to God. (2.) He therefore went to Tarshish, to Tarsus in Cilicia (so some), probably because he had friends and relations there, with whom he hoped for some time to sojourn. He went to Joppa, a famous seaport in the land of Israel, in quest of a ship bound for Tarshish, and there he found one. Providence seemed to favour his design, and give him an opportunity to escape. We may be out of the way of duty and yet may meet with a favourable gale. The ready way is not always the right way. He found the ship just ready to weigh anchor perhaps, and to set sail for Tarshish, and so he lost no time. Or, perhaps, he went to Tarshish because he found the ship going thither; otherwise all places were alike to him. He did not think himself out of his way, the way he would go, provided he was not in his way, the way he should go. So he <hi type="italic">paid the fare thereof;</hi> for he did not regard the charge, so he could but gain his point, and get to a distance <hi type="italic">from the presence of the Lord.</hi> He went <hi type="italic">with them,</hi> with the mariners, with the passengers, with the merchants, whoever they were that were going to Tarshish. Jonah, forgetting his dignity as well as his duty, herded with them, and <hi type="italic">went down</hi> into the ship to go <hi type="italic">with them to Tarshish.</hi> See what the best of men are when God leaves them to themselves, and what need we have, when the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> comes to us, to have the <hi type="italic">Spirit of the Lord</hi> come along with the word, to bring every thought within us into obedience to it. The prophet Isaiah owns that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he was not <hi type="italic">rebellious,</hi> neither <hi type="italic">turned away back,</hi> because God not only spoke to him, but <hi type="italic">opened his ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.5">Isa. l. 5</reference>. Let us learn hence to <hi type="italic">cease from man,</hi> and not to be too confident either of ourselves or others in a time of trial; but <hi type="italic">let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.</hi>
entries.d7bfb93ec989e9035a0d027ad6ce2baf79ed2f3b: <div eID="gen20297" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet in the Storm; The Prophet Convicted by the Lot. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 840.)</title> <div sID="gen20298" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sent out a great wind into the sea, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea, so that the ship was like to be broken. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god, and cast forth the wares that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the ship into the sea, to lighten <hi type="italic">it</hi> of them. But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep. <hi type="super">6</hi> So the ship-master came to him, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O sleeper? arise, call upon thy God, if so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not. <hi type="super">7</hi> And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon <reference osisRef="Jonah.8">Jonah.   8</reference> Then said they unto him, Tell us, we pray thee, for whose cause this evil <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon us; What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine occupation? and whence comest thou? what <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy country? and of what people <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou? <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said unto them, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a Hebrew; and I fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry <hi type="italic">land.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him, Why hast thou done this? For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because he had told them. <div eID="gen20298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20299" type="x-p"/> When Jonah was set on ship-board, and under sail for Tarshish, he thought himself safe enough; but here we find him pursued and overtaken, discovered and convicted as a deserter from God, as one that had <hi type="italic">run his colours.</hi> <div eID="gen20299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20300" type="x-p"/> I. God sends a pursuer after him, <hi type="italic">a mighty tempest in the sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.4">v. 4</reference>. God has the <hi type="italic">winds in his treasure</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>), and out of these treasures God <hi type="italic">sent forth,</hi> he <hi type="italic">cast forth</hi> (so the word is), with force and violence, <hi type="italic">a great wind into the sea;</hi> even <hi type="italic">stormy winds fulfil his word,</hi> and are often the messengers of his wrath; he <hi type="italic">gathers the winds in his fist</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Prov. xxx. 4</reference>), where he holds them, and whence he squeezes them when he pleases; for though, as to us, the <hi type="italic">wind blows where it listeth,</hi> yet not as to God, but where he directs. The effect of this wind as <hi type="italic">a mighty tempest;</hi> for when the winds rise the waves rise. Note, Sin brings storms and tempests into the soul, into the family, into churches and nations; it is a disquieting disturbing thing. The tempest prevailed to such a degree that <hi type="italic">the ship was likely to be broken;</hi> the mariners expected no other; <hi type="italic">that ship</hi> (so some read it), that and no other. Other ships were upon the same sea at the same time, yet, it should seem, that ship in which Jonah was was tossed more than any other and was more in danger. This wind was sent after Jonah, to fetch him back again to God and to his duty; and it is a great mercy to be reclaimed and called home when we go astray, though it be by a tempest. <div eID="gen20300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20301" type="x-p"/> II. The ship's crew were alarmed by this mighty tempest, but Jonah only, the person concerned, was unconcerned, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.5">v. 5</reference>. The mariners were affected with their danger, though it was not with them that God has this controversy. 1. They were <hi type="italic">afraid;</hi> though, their business leading them to be very much conversant with dangers of this kind, they used to make light of them, yet now the oldest and stoutest of them began to tremble, being apprehensive that there was something more than ordinary in this tempest, so suddenly did it rise, so strongly did it rage. Note, God can strike a terror upon the most daring, and make even <hi type="italic">great men and chief captains</hi> call for shelter from rocks and mountains. 2. They <hi type="italic">cried every man unto his god;</hi> this was the effect of their fear. Many will not be brought to prayer till they are frightened to it; he that would learn to pray, let him go to sea. <hi type="italic">Lord, in trouble they have visited thee. Every man</hi> of them prayed; they were not some praying and others reviling, but every man engaged; as the danger was general, so was the address to heaven; there was not one praying for them all, but every one for himself. They cried <hi type="italic">every man to his god,</hi> the god of his country or city, or his own tutelar deity; it is a testimony against atheism that every man had a god, and had the belief of a God; but it is an instance of the folly of paganism that they had gods many, every man the god he had a fancy for, whereas there can be but one God, there needs to be no more. But, though they had lost that dictate of the light of nature that there is but <hi type="italic">one God,</hi> they still were governed by that direction of the law of nature that God is to be prayed to (<hi type="italic">Should not a people seek under their God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>), and that he is especially to be prayed to when we are in distress and danger. <hi type="italic">Call upon me in the time of trouble. Is any afflicted?</hi> Is any frightened? <hi type="italic">Let him pray.</hi> 3. Their prayers for deliverance were seconded with endeavours, and, having called upon their gods to help them, they did what they could to help themselves; for that is the rule, <hi type="italic">Help thyself and God will help thee.</hi> They <hi type="italic">cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it of them,</hi> as Paul's mariners in a like case cast forth even the <hi type="italic">tackling of the ship,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">wheat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.27.18-Acts.27.19">Acts xxvii. 18, 19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.27.38">38</reference>. They were making a trading voyage, as it should seem, and were laden with many goods and much merchandise, by which they hoped to get gain; but now they are content to suffer loss by throwing them overboard. to save their lives. See how powerful the natural love of life is. <hi type="italic">Skin for skin,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all that a man has, will he give for it.</hi> And shall we not put a like value upon the spiritual life, the life of the soul, reckoning that the gain of all the world cannot countervail the loss of the soul? See the vanity of worldly wealth, and the uncertainty of its continuance with us. Riches make themselves wings and fly away; nay, and the case may be such that we may be under a necessity of making wings for them, and driving them away, as here, when they could not be <hi type="italic">kept for the owners thereof</hi> but to their hurt, so that they themselves are glad to be rid of them, and sink that which otherwise would sink them, though they have no prospect of ever recovering it. Oh that men would be thus wise for their souls, and would be willing to part with that wealth, pleasure, and honour which they cannot keep without <hi type="italic">making shipwreck of faith and a good conscience</hi> and ruining their souls for ever! Those that thus quit their temporal interests for the securing of their spiritual welfare will be unspeakable gainers at last; for what they lose upon those terms they shall find again to life eternal. But where is Jonah all this while? One would have expected gone down into his cabin, nay, into <hi type="italic">the hold, between the sides of the ship,</hi> and there he lies, and is <hi type="italic">fast asleep;</hi> neither the noise without, nor the sense of guilt within, awoke him. Perhaps for some time before he had avoiding sleeping, for fear of God's speaking to him again in a dream; and now that he imagined himself out of the reach of that danger, he slept so much the more soundly. Note, Sin is of a stupifying nature, and we are concerned to <hi type="italic">take heed lest at any time our hearts be hardened by the deceitfulness of it.</hi> It is the policy of Satan, when by his temptations he has drawn men from God and their duty, to rock them asleep in carnal security, that they may not be sensible of their misery and danger. It concerns us all to <hi type="italic">watch therefore.</hi> <div eID="gen20301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20302" type="x-p"/> III. The master of the ship called Jonah up to his prayers, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.6">v. 6</reference>. The <hi type="italic">ship-master came to him,</hi> and bade him for shame get up, both to <hi type="italic">pray for life</hi> and to <hi type="italic">prepare for death;</hi> he gave him, 1. A just and necessary chiding: <hi type="italic">What meanest thou, O sleeper?</hi> Here we commend the ship-master, who gave him this reproof; for, though he was a stranger to him, he was, for the present, as one of his family; and whoever has a precious soul we must help, as we can, to <hi type="italic">save it from death.</hi> We pity Jonah, who needed this reproof; as a prophet of the Lord, if he had been in his place, he might have been reproving the king of Nineveh, but, being out of the way of his duty, he does himself lie open to the reproofs of a sorry ship-master. See how men by their sin and folly diminish themselves and make themselves mean. Yet we must admire God's goodness in sending him this seasonable reproof, for it was the first step towards his recovery, as the crowing of the cock was to Peter. Note, Those that sleep in a storm may well be asked what they mean. 2. A pertinent word of advice: "<hi type="italic">Arise, call upon thy God;</hi> we are here crying every man to his god, why dost not thou get up and cry to thine? Art not thou equally concerned with the rest both in the danger dreaded and in the deliverance desired?" Note, The devotions of others should quicken ours; and those who hope to share in a common mercy ought in all reason to contribute their quota towards the prayers and supplications that are made for it. In times of public distress, if we have any interest at the throne of grace, we ought to improve it for the public good. And the servants of God themselves have sometimes need to be called and stirred up to this part of their duty. 3. A good reason for this advice: <hi type="italic">If so be that God will think upon us, that we perish not.</hi> It should seem, the many gods they called upon were considered by them only as mediators between them and the supreme God, and intercessors for them with him; for the ship-master speaks of one God still, from whom he expected relief. To engage prayer, he suggested that the danger was very great and imminent: "We are all likely to <hi type="italic">perish;</hi> there is but a step between us and death, and that just ready to be stepped." Yet he suggested that there was some hope remaining that their destruction might be prevented and they might <hi type="italic">not perish.</hi> While there is still life there is hope, and while there is hope there is room for prayer. He suggested also that it was God only that could effect their deliverance, and it must come from his power and his pity. "If he <hi type="italic">think upon us,</hi> and act for us, we may yet be saved." And therefore to him we must look, and in him we must put our trust, when the danger is ever so imminent. <div eID="gen20302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20303" type="x-p"/> IV. Jonah is found out to be the cause of the storm. <div eID="gen20303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20304" type="x-p"/> 1. The mariners observed so much peculiar and uncommon either in the storm itself or in their own distress by it that they concluded it was a messenger of divine justice sent to arrest some one of those that were in that ship, as having been guilty of some enormous crime, judging as the barbarous people (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.4">Acts xxviii. 4</reference>), "<hi type="italic">no doubt one of us is a murderer,</hi> or guilty of sacrilege, or perjury, or the like, who is thus <hi type="italic">pursued</hi> by the <hi type="italic">vengeance of the sea,</hi> and it is for his sake that we all suffer." Even the light of nature teaches that in extraordinary judgments the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against some extraordinary sins and sinners. Whatever evil is upon us at any time we must conclude <hi type="italic">there is a cause</hi> for it; there is evil done by us, or else this evil would not be upon us; there is a ground for God's controversy. <div eID="gen20304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20305" type="x-p"/> 2. They determined to refer it to the lot which of them was the criminal that had occasioned this storm: <hi type="italic">Let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause the evil is upon us.</hi> None of them suspected himself, or said, <hi type="italic">Is it I,</hi> Lord; <hi type="italic">is it I?</hi> But they suspected one another, and would find out the man. Note, It is a desirable thing, when any evil is upon us, to know for what cause it is upon us, that what is amiss may be amended, and, the grievance being redressed, the grief may be removed. In order to this we must look up to heaven, and pray, Lord, <hi type="italic">show me wherefore thou contendest with me; that which I see not teach thou me.</hi> These mariners desired to know the person that was the dead weight in their ship, the accursed thing, that that one man might <hi type="italic">die for the people</hi> and that the whole ship <hi type="italic">might not be lost;</hi> this was not only expedient, but highly just. In order to this they cast lots, by which they appealed to the judgment of God, to whom <hi type="italic">all hearts are open, and from whom no secret is hid,</hi> agreeing to acquiesce in his discovery and determination, and to take that for true which the lot spoke; for they knew by the light of nature, what the scripture tells us, that <hi type="italic">the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposal thereof is of the Lord.</hi> Even the heathen looked upon the casting of lots to be a sacred thing, to be done with seriousness and solemnity, and not to be made a sport of. It is a shame for Christians if they have not a like reverence for an appeal to Providence. <div eID="gen20305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20306" type="x-p"/> 3. The <hi type="italic">lot fell upon Jonah,</hi> who could have saved them this trouble if he would but have told them what his own conscience told him, <hi type="italic">Thou are the man;</hi> but as is usual with criminals, he never confesses till he finds he cannot help it, till <hi type="italic">the lot falls upon him.</hi> We may suppose there were those in the ship who, upon other accounts, were greater sinners than Jonah, and yet he is the man that the tempest pursues and that the lot pitches upon; for it is his own child, his own servant, that the parent, that the master, corrects, if they do amiss; others that offend he leaves to the law. The storm is sent after Jonah, because God has work for him to do, and it is sent to fetch him back to it. Note, God has many ways of bringing to light concealed sins and sinners, and making manifest that folly which was thought to be hidden from the eyes of all living. God's right hand will find out all his servants that desert him, as well as all his enemies that have designs against him; yea, though they flee to the uttermost parts of the sea, or go down to the sides of the ship. <div eID="gen20306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20307" type="x-p"/> 4. Jonah is hereupon brought under examination before the master and mariners. He was a stranger; none of them could say that they knew the prisoner, or had any thing to lay to his charge, and therefore they must extort a confession from him and judge him <hi type="italic">out of his own mouth;</hi> and for this there needed no rack, the shipwreck they were in danger of was sufficient to frighten him, so as to make him tell the truth. Though it was discovered by the lot that he was the person for whose sake they were thus damaged and exposed, yet they did not fly outrageously upon him, as one would fear they might have done, but calmly and mildly enquired into his case. There is a compassion due to offenders when they are discovered and convicted. They give him no hard words, but, "<hi type="italic">Tell us, we pray thee,</hi> what is the matter?" Two things they enquire of him:—(1.) Whether he would himself own that he was the person for whose sake the storm was sent, as the lot had intimated: "<hi type="italic">Tell us for whose cause this evil is upon us;</hi> is it indeed for thy cause, and, if so, <hi type="italic">for what cause?</hi> What is this offence for which thou art thus prosecuted?" Perhaps the gravity and decency of Jonah's aspect and behaviour made them suspect that the lot had missed its man, had missed its mark, and therefore they would not trust it, unless he would himself own his guilt; they therefore begged of him that he would satisfy them in this matter. Note, Those that would find out the cause of their troubles must not only begin, but pursue the enquiry, must descend to particulars and <hi type="italic">accomplish a diligent search.</hi> (2.) What his character was, both as to his calling and as to his country. [1.] They enquire concerning his calling: <hi type="italic">What is thy occupation?</hi> This was a proper question to be put to a vagrant. Perhaps they suspected his calling to be such as might bring this trouble upon them: "Art thou a diviner, a sorcerer, a student in the black art? Hast thou been conjuring for this wind? Or what business are thou now going on? It is like Balaam's, to curse any of God's people, and is this wind send to stop thee?" [2.] They enquire concerning his country. One asked, <hi type="italic">Whence comest thou?</hi> Another, not having patience to stay for an answer to that, asked, <hi type="italic">What is thy country?</hi> A third to the same purport, "<hi type="italic">Of what people art thou?</hi> Art thou of the Chaldeans," that were noted for divination, "or of the Arabians," that were noted for stealing? They wished to know of what country he was, that, knowing who was the god of his country, they might guess whether he was one that could do them any kindness in this storm. <div eID="gen20307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20308" type="x-p"/> 5. In answer to these interrogatories Jonah makes a full discovery. (1.) Did they enquire concerning his country? He tells them he is <hi type="italic">a Hebrew</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.9">v. 9</reference>), not only of the nation of Israel, but of their religion, which they received from their fathers. He is a Hebrew, and therefore is the more ashamed to own that he is a criminal; for the sins of Hebrews, that make such a profession of religion and enjoy such privileges, are greater than the sins of others, and more exceedingly sinful. (2.) Did they enquire concerning his calling—<hi type="italic">What is thy occupation?</hi> In answer to that he gives an account of his religion, for that was his calling, that was his occupation, that was it that he made a business of: "<hi type="italic">I fear the Lord Jehovah;</hi> that is the God I worship, the God I pray to, even <hi type="italic">the God of heaven,</hi> the sovereign Lord of all, that has <hi type="italic">made the sea and the dry land</hi> and has command of both." Not the god of one particular country, which they enquired after, and such as the gods were that they had been every man calling upon, but <hi type="italic">the God of the whole earth,</hi> who, having made both the sea and the dry land, makes what work he pleases in both and makes what use he pleases of both. This he mentions, not only as condemning himself for his folly, in fleeing from the presence of this God, but as designing to bring these mariners from the worship and service of their many gods to the knowledge and obedience of the one only living and true God. When we are among those that are strangers to us we should do what we can to bring them acquainted with God, by being ready upon all occasions to own our relation to him and our reverence for him. (3.) Did they enquire concerning his crime, for which he is now persecuted? He owns that he <hi type="italic">fled from the presence of the Lord,</hi> that he was here running away from his duty, and the storm was sent to fetch him back. We have reason to think that he told them this with sorrow and shame, justifying God and condemning himself and intimating to the mariners what a great God Jehovah is, who could send such a messenger as this tempest was after a runagate servant. <div eID="gen20308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20309" type="x-p"/> 6. We are told what impression this made upon the mariners: <hi type="italic">The men were exceedingly afraid,</hi> and justly, for they perceived, (1.) That God was angry, even that God that made <hi type="italic">the sea and the dry land.</hi> This tempest comes from the hand of an offended justice, and therefore they have reason to fear it will go hard with them. Judgments inflicted for some particular sin have a peculiar weight and terror in them. (2.) That God was angry with one that feared and worshipped him, only for once running from his work in particular instance; this made them afraid for themselves. "If a prophet of the Lord be thus severely punished for one offence, what will become of us that have been guilty of so many, and great, and heinous offences?" If <hi type="italic">the righteous be</hi> thus <hi type="italic">scarcely saved,</hi> and for a single act of disobedience thus closely pursued, <hi type="italic">where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.18">1 Pet. iv. 17, 18</reference>. They said to him, "<hi type="italic">Why hast thou done this?</hi> If thou fearest the God that <hi type="italic">made the sea and the dry land,</hi> why wast thou such a fool as to think thou couldst flee from his presence? What an absurd unaccountable thing is it!" <hi type="italic">Thus he was reproved,</hi> as Abraham by Abimelech (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.16">Gen. xx. 16</reference>); for if the professors of religion do a wrong thing they must expect to hear of it from those that make no such profession. "<hi type="italic">Why hast thou done this to us?</hi>" (so it may be taken) "Why has thou involved us in the prosecution?" Note, Those that commit a willful sin know not how far the mischievous consequences of it may reach, nor what mischief may be done by it.
entries.6aa2b04303430e53c47866599a3e4865d6c04a04: <div eID="gen20309" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet Confesses His Folly; The Prophet Reads His Own Doom; The Prophet Cast into the Sea; Jonah's Preservation in the Fish's Belly. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  840.)</title> <div sID="gen20310" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said they unto him, What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm unto us? for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he said unto them, Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you: for I know that for my sake this great tempest <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon you. <hi type="super">13</hi> Nevertheless the men rowed hard to bring <hi type="italic">it</hi> to the land; but they could not: for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them. <hi type="super">14</hi> Wherefore they cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, We beseech thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , we beseech thee, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not upon us innocent blood: for thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , hast done as it pleased thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> So they took up Jonah, and cast him forth into the sea: and the sea ceased from her raging. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then the men feared the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and made vows. <hi type="super">17</hi> Now the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. <div eID="gen20310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20311" type="x-p"/> It is plain that Jonah is the man for whose sake this evil is upon them, but the discovery of him to be so was not sufficient to answer the demands of this tempest; they had found him out, but something more was to be done, for still <hi type="italic">the sea wrought and was tempestuous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.11">v. 11</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.13">v. 13</reference>), it <hi type="italic">grew more and more tempestuous</hi> (so the margin reads it); for if we discover sin to be the cause of our troubles, and do not forsake it, we do but make bad worse. Therefore they went on with the prosecution. <div eID="gen20311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20312" type="x-p"/> I. They enquired of Jonah himself what he thought they must do with him (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">What shall we do unto thee, that the sea may be calm to us?</hi> They perceived that Jonah is a prophet of the Lord, and therefore will not do any thing, no, not in his own case, without consulting him. He appears to be a delinquent, but he appears also to be a penitent, and therefore they will not insult over him, nor offer him any rudeness. Note, We ought to act with great tenderness towards those that are overtaken in a fault and are brought into distress by it. They would not <hi type="italic">cast him into the sea</hi> if he could think of any other expedient by which to <hi type="italic">save the ship.</hi> Or, perhaps, thus they would show how plain the case was, that there was no remedy but he must be thrown overboard; let him be his own judge as he had been his own accuser, and he himself will say so. Note, When sin has raised a storm, and laid us under the tokens of God's displeasure, we are concerned to enquire what we shall do that the sea may be calm; and what shall we do? We must pray and believe, when we are in a storm, and study to answer the end for which it was sent, and then the storm shall become a calm. But especially we must consider what is to be done to the sin that raised the storm; that must be discovered, and penitently confessed; that must be detested, disclaimed, and utterly forsaken. What have I to do any more with it? Crucify it, crucify it, for this evil it has done. <div eID="gen20312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20313" type="x-p"/> II. Jonah reads his own doom (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea.</hi> He would not himself leap into the sea, but he put himself into their hands, to cast him into the sea, and assured them that then the <hi type="italic">sea would be calm,</hi> and not otherwise. He proposed this, in tenderness to the mariners, that they might not suffer for his sake. "<hi type="italic">Let thy hand be upon me</hi>" (says David, <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.17">1 Chron. xxi. 17</reference>), "who am guilty; let me die for my own sin, but let not the innocent suffer for it." This is the language of true penitents, who earnestly desire that none but themselves may ever smart, or fare the worse, for their sins and follies. He proposed it likewise in submission to the will of God, who sent this tempest in pursuit of him; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> judged himself to be cast into the sea, because to that he plainly saw God judging him, that he might not be <hi type="italic">judged of the Lord</hi> to eternal misery. Note, Those who are truly humbled for sin will cheerfully submit to the will of God, even in a sentence of death itself. If Jonah sees this to be the punishment of his iniquity, he accepts it, he subjects himself to it, and justifies God in it. No matter though the <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> be <hi type="italic">destroyed,</hi> no matter how it is destroyed, so that the <hi type="italic">spirit may</hi> be <hi type="italic">but saved in the day of the Lord Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">1 Cor. v. 5</reference>. The reason he gives is, <hi type="italic">For I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you.</hi> See how ready Jonah is to take all the guilt upon himself, and to look upon all the trouble as theirs: "It is purely for my sake, who have sinned, that this tempest is upon you; therefore cast me forth into the sea; for," 1. "I deserve it. I have wickedly departed from my God, and it is upon my account that he is angry with you. Surely I am unworthy to breathe in that air which for my sake has been hurried with winds, to live in that ship which for my sake has been thus tossed. Cast me into the sea after the wares which for my sake you have thrown into it. Drowning is too good for me; a single death is punishment too little for such a complicated offence." 2. "Therefore there is no way of having the sea calm. If it is I that have raised the storm, it is not casting the wares into the sea that will lay it again; no, you must cast me thither." When conscience is awakened, and a storm raised there, nothing will turn it into a calm but parting with the sin that occasioned the disturbance, and abandoning that. It is not parting with our money that will pacify conscience; no, it is the Jonah that be thrown overboard. Jonah is herein a type of Christ, that he <hi type="italic">gives his life a ransom for many;</hi> but with this material difference, that the storm Jonah gave himself up to still was of his own raising, but that storm which Christ gave himself up to still was of our raising. Yet, as Jonah delivered himself up to be cast into a raging sea that it might be calm, so did our Lord Jesus, when he died that we might live. <div eID="gen20313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20314" type="x-p"/> III. The poor mariners did what they could to save themselves from the necessity of throwing Jonah into the sea, but all in vain (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They rowed hard to bring the ship to the land,</hi> that, if they must part with Jonah, they might set him safely on shore; <hi type="italic">but they could not.</hi> All their pains were to no purpose; <hi type="italic">for the sea wrought</hi> harder than they could, and <hi type="italic">was tempestuous against them,</hi> so that they could by no means <hi type="italic">make the land.</hi> If they thought sometimes that they had gained their point, they were quickly thrown off to sea again. Still their ship was overladen; their lightening it of the wares made it never the lighter as long as Jonah was in it. And, besides, they rowed against wind and tide, the wind of God's vengeance, the tide of his counsels; and it is in vain to contend with God, in vain to think of saving ourselves any other way than by destroying our sins. By this it appears that these mariners were very loth to execute Jonah's sentence upon himself, though they knew it was for his sake that this tempest was upon them. They were thus very backward to it partly from a dread of bringing upon themselves the guilt of blood, and partly from a compassion they could not but have for poor Jonah, as a good man, as a man in distress, and as a man of sincerity. Note, The more sinners humble and abase themselves, judge and condemn themselves, the more likely they are to find pity both with God and man. The more forward Jonah was to say, <hi type="italic">Cast me into the sea,</hi> the more backward they were to do it. <div eID="gen20314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20315" type="x-p"/> IV. When they found it necessary to cast Jonah into the sea they first prayed to God that the guilt of his blood might not lie upon them, nor be laid to their charge, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.14">v. 14</reference>. When they found it in vain to row hard they quitted their oars and went to their prayers: <hi type="italic">Wherefore they cried unto the Lord,</hi> unto <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> the true and living God, and no more to the <hi type="italic">gods many.</hi> and <hi type="italic">lords many,</hi> that the had <hi type="italic">cried to,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.5">v. 5</reference>. They prayed to the <hi type="italic">God of Israel,</hi> being now convinced, by the providences of God concerning Jonah and the information he had given them, that he is God <hi type="italic">alone.</hi> Having determined to cast Jonah into the sea, they first enter a protestation in the court of heaven that they do not do it willingly, much less maliciously, or with any design to be revenged upon him because it was for his sake that this tempest was upon them. No; <hi type="italic">his god forgive him,</hi> as <hi type="italic">they do!</hi> But they are forced to do it <hi type="italic">se defendendo—in self-defence,</hi> having no other way to save their own lives; and they do it as ministers of justice, both God and himself having sentenced him to <hi type="italic">so great a death.</hi> They <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> present a humble petition to the God whom Jonah feared, that they might not <hi type="italic">perish for his life.</hi> See, 1. What a fear they had of contracting the guilt of blood, especially the blood of one that feared God, and worshipped him, and had fellowship with him, as they perceived Jonah had, though in a single instance he had been faulty. Natural conscience cannot but have a dread of blood-guiltiness, and make men very earnest in prayer, as David was, to be delivered from it, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.14">Ps. li. 14</reference>. So they were here: <hi type="italic">We beseech thee, O Lord! we beseech thee, lay not upon us innocent blood.</hi> They are now as earnest in praying to be saved from the peril of sin as they were before in praying to be saved from the peril of the sea, especially because Jonah appeared to them to be no ordinary person, but a very good man, a man of God, a worshipper of the great Creator of heaven and earth, upon which account even these rude mariners conceived a veneration for him, and trembled at the thought of taking away his life. Innocent blood is precious, but saints' blood, prophets' blood, is much more precious, and so those will find to their cost that any way bring themselves under the guilt of it. The mariners saw Jonah pursued by divine vengeance, and yet could not without horror think of being his executioners. Though his God has a controversy with him, yet, think they, <hi type="italic">Let not our hand be upon him.</hi> The Israelites were at this time killing the prophets for doing their duty (witness Jezebel's late persecution), and were prodigal of their lives, which is aggravated by the tenderness these heathens had for one whom they perceived to be a prophet, though he was now out of the way of his duty. 2. What a fear they had of incurring the wrath of God; they were jealous lest he should be angry if they should be the death of Jonah, for he had said, <hi type="italic">Touch not my anointed, and do my prophets no harm;</hi> it is at your peril if you do. "Lord," say they, "<hi type="italic">let us not perish for this man's life.</hi> Let it not be such a fatal dilemma to us. We see we must perish if we spare his life; Oh let us not perish for taking away his life." And their plea is good: "<hi type="italic">For thou, O Lord! hast done as it pleased thee;</hi> thou had laid us under a necessity of doing it; the wind that pursued him, the lot that discovered him, were both under thy direction, which we are herein governed by; we are but the instruments of Providence, and it is sorely against our will that we do it; but we must say, <hi type="italic">The will of the Lord be done.</hi>" Note, When we are manifestly led by Providence to do things contrary to our own inclinations, and quite beyond our own intentions, it will be some satisfaction to us to be able to say, <hi type="italic">Thou, O Lord! has done as it pleased thee.</hi> And, if God please himself, we ought to be satisfied though he do not please us. <div eID="gen20315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20316" type="x-p"/> V. Having deprecated the guilt they dreaded, they proceeded to execution (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">They took up Jonah,</hi> and <hi type="italic">cast him forth into the sea.</hi> They cast him out of their ship, out of their company, and cast him into the sea, a raging stormy sea, that cried, "Give, give; surrender the traitor, or expect no peace." We may well think what confusion and amazement poor Jonah was in when he saw himself ready to be hurried into the presence of that God as a Judge whose presence as a Master he was now fleeing from. Note, Those know not what ruin they run upon that run away from God. <hi type="italic">Woe unto them! for they have fled from me.</hi> When sin is the Jonah that raises the storm, that must thus be cast forth into the sea; we must abandon it, and be the death of it, must drown that which otherwise will <hi type="italic">drown us in destruction and perdition.</hi> And if we thus by a thorough repentance and reformation cast our sins forth into the sea, never to recall them or return to them again, God will by pardoning mercy subdue our iniquities, and <hi type="italic">cast them into the depths of the sea</hi> too, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">Mic. vii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen20316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20317" type="x-p"/> VI. The throwing of Jonah into the sea immediately put an end to the storm. The sea has what she came for, and therefore rests contended; she <hi type="italic">ceases from her raging.</hi> It is an instance of the sovereign power of God that he can soon turn the storm into a calm, and of the equity of his government that when the end of an affliction is answered and attained the affliction shall immediately be removed. He will not contend for ever, will not contend any longer till we submit ourselves and give up the cause. If we turn from our sins, he will soon turn from his anger. <div eID="gen20317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20318" type="x-p"/> VII. The mariners were hereby more confirmed in their belief that Jonah's God was the only true God (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then the men feared the Lord with a great fear,</hi> were possessed with a deep veneration for the God of Israel, and came to a resolution that they would worship him only for the future; for <hi type="italic">there is no other God that can</hi> destroy, that <hi type="italic">can deliver, after this sort.</hi> When they saw the power of God in raising and laying the tempest, when they saw his justice upon Jonah his own servant, and when they saw his goodness to them in saving them from the brink of ruin, <hi type="italic">then they feared the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer. v. 22</reference>. As an evidence of their fear of him, they <hi type="italic">offered sacrifice</hi> to him when they came ashore again in the land of Israel, and for the present made vows that they would do so, in thankfulness for their deliverance, and to make atonement for their souls. Or, perhaps, they had something yet on board which might be for a sacrifice to God immediately. Or it may be meant of the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise, with which God is better pleased than with that of an ox or bullock that has horns and hoofs. See <reference osisRef="Ps.107.2">Ps. cvii. 2</reference>, &c. We must make vows, not only when we are in the pursuit of mercy, but, which is much more generous, when we have received mercy, as those that are still studying what we shall render. <div eID="gen20318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20319" type="x-p"/> VIII. Jonah's life, after all, is saved by a miracle, and we shall hear of him again for all this. In the midst of judgment God <hi type="italic">remembers mercy.</hi> Jonah shall be worse frightened than hurt, not so much punished for his sin as reduced to his duty. Though he flees from the presence of the Lord, and seems to fall into his avenging hands, yet God has more work for him to do, and therefore has <hi type="italic">prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">a whale</hi> our Saviour calls it (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.40">Matt. xii. 40</reference>), one of the largest sorts of whales, that have wider throats than others, in the belly of which has sometimes been found the dead body of a man in armour. Particular notice is taken, in the history of creation, of God's <hi type="italic">creating great whales</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.21">Gen. i. 21</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi> in the waters <hi type="italic">made to play therein,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Ps. civ. 26</reference>. But God finds work for this leviathan, has <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> him, has <hi type="italic">numbered</hi> him (so the word is), has appointed him to be Jonah's receiver and deliverer. Note, God has command of all the creatures, and can make any of them serve his designs of mercy to his people, even the fishes of the sea, that are most from under man's cognizance, even the great whales, that are altogether from under man's government. This fish was prepared, lay ready under water close by the ship, that he might keep Jonah from sinking to the bottom, and save him alive, though he deserved to die. Let us <hi type="italic">stand still and see this salvation of the Lord,</hi> and admire his power, that he could thus save a drowning man, and his pity, that he would thus save one that was running from him and had offended him. It was of the Lord's mercies that Jonah was not now consumed. The fish swallowed up Jonah, not to devour him, but to protect him. <hi type="italic">Out of the eater comes forth meat;</hi> for Jonah was alive and well <hi type="italic">in the belly of the fish three days and three nights,</hi> not consumed by the heat of the animal, nor suffocated for want of air. It is granted that to nature this was impossible, but not to the God of nature, with whom all things are possible. Jonah by this miraculous preservation was designed to be made, 1. A monument of divine mercy, for the encouragement of those that have sinned, and gone away from God, to return and repent. 2. A successful preacher to Nineveh; and this miracle wrought for his deliverance, if the tidings of it reached Nineveh, would contribute to his success. 3. An illustrious type of Christ, who was buried and rose again according to the scriptures (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.4">1 Cor. xv. 4</reference>), according to this scripture, for, <hi type="italic">as Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale's belly, so was the Son of man three days and three nights in the heart of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.12.40">Matt. xii. 40</reference>. Jonah's burial was a figure of Christ's. God prepared Jonah's grave, so he did Christ's, when it was long before ordained that he should <hi type="italic">make his grave with the rich,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Isa. liii. 9</reference>. Was Jonah's grave a strange one, a new one? So was Christ's, one in which never man before was laid. Was Jonah there the best part of three days and three nights? So was Christ; but both in order to their rising again for the bringing of the doctrine of repentance to the Gentile world. <hi type="italic">Come, see the place where the Lord lay.</hi>  <chapter eID="Jonah.1"/> <div eID="gen20319" type="x-p"/>

entries.2105a0e235380ea8dc7e0ba8499637b79d9b5612: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12669"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen23427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jonah was the son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher in Zebulun (called Gittah-hepher in <reference osisRef="Josh.19.10-Josh.19.13">Jos 19:10-13</reference>), so that he belonged to the kingdom of the ten tribes, not to Judah. His date is to be gathered from <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25-2Kgs.14.27">2Ki 14:25-27</reference>, "He (Jeroboam II) restored the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath unto the sea of the plain, according to the word of the Lord God of Israel, which He spake by the hand of His servant Jonah, the son of Amittai, the prophet, which was of Gath-hepher. For the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter: for there was not any shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel. And the Lord said not that He would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven: but He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash." Now as this prophecy of Jonah was given at a time when Israel was at the lowest point of depression, when "there was not any shut up or left," that is, confined or left at large, none to act as a helper for Israel, it cannot have been given in Jeroboam's reign, which was marked by prosperity, for in it Syria was worsted in fulfilment of the prophecy, and Israel raised to its former "greatness." It must have been, therefore, in the early part of the reign of Joash, Jeroboam's father, who had found Israel in subjection to Syria, but had raised it by victories which were followed up so successfully by Jeroboam. Thus Jonah was the earliest of the prophets, and close upon Elisha, who died in Joash's reign, having just before his death given a token prophetical of the thrice defeat of Syria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.14-2Kgs.13.21">2Ki 13:14-21</reference>). Hosea and Amos prophesied also in the reign of Jeroboam II, but towards the closing part of his forty-one years' reign. The transactions in the Book of Jonah probably occurred in the latter part of his life; if so, the book is not much older than part of the writings of Hosea and Amos. The use of the third person is no argument against Jonah himself being the writer: for the sacred writers in mentioning themselves do so in the third person (compare <reference osisRef="John.19.26">Joh 19:26</reference>). Nor is the use of the past tense (<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.3">Jon 3:3</reference>, "Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city") a proof that Nineveh's greatness was past when the Book of Jonah was being written; it is simply used to carry on the negative uniformly,--</hi>"the word of the Lord came to Jonah ... so Jonah arose ... now Nineveh was," &c. (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.1">Jon 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.3">3:3</reference>). The mention of its greatness proves rather that the book was written at an early date, before the Israelites had that intimate knowledge of it which they must have had soon afterwards through frequent Assyrian inroads.<div eID="gen23427" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23426" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23428" type="x-p"/> As early as Julian and Porphyry, pagans ridiculed the credulity of Christians in believing the deliverance of Jonah by a fish. Some infidels have derived it from the heathen fable of the deliverance of Andromeda from a sea monster by Perseus [Apollodorus, The Library, 2.4,3]; or from that of Arion the musician thrown into the sea by sailors, and carried safe to shore on a dolphin [Herodotus, History, 1.24]; or from that of Hercules, who sprang into the jaws of a sea monster, and was three days in its belly, when he undertook to save Hesione [Diodorus Siculus, Historical Library, 4.42; Homer, The Iliad, 20.145; 21.442]. Probably the heathen fables are, vice versa, corruptions of the sacred narrative, if there be any connection. Jerome states that near Joppa lay rocks, pointed out as those to which Andromeda was bound when exposed to the sea monster. This fable implies the likelihood of the story of Jonah having passed through the Phoenicians in a corrupted form to Greece. That the account of Jonah is history, and not parable (as rationalists represent), appears from our Lord's reference to it, in which the personal existence, miraculous fate, and prophetical office of Jonah are explicitly asserted: "No sign shall be given but the sign of the prophet Jonas: for, as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly, so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.39">Mt 12:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.40">40</reference>). The Lord recognizes his being in the belly of the fish as a "sign," that is, a real miracle, typical of a similar event in His own history; and assumes the execution of the prophet's commission to Nineveh, "The men of Nineveh ... repented at the preaching of Jonas; and behold, a greater than Jonas is here" (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.41">Mt 12:41</reference>).<div eID="gen23428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23429" type="x-p"/> It seemed strange to Kimchi, a Jew himself, that the Book of Jonah is among the Scriptures, as the only prophecy in it concerns Nineveh, a heathen city, and makes no mention of Israel, which is referred to by every other prophet. The reason seems to be: a tacit reproof of Israel is intended; a heathen people were ready to repent at the first preaching of the prophet, a stranger to them; but Israel, who boasted of being God's elect, repented not, though warned by their own prophets at all seasons. This was an anticipatory streak of light before the dawn of the full "light to lighten the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Lu 2:32</reference>). Jonah is himself a strange paradox: a prophet of God, and yet a runaway from God: a man drowned, and yet alive: a preacher of repentance, yet one that repines at repentance. Yet Jonah, saved from the jaws of death himself on repentance, was the fittest to give a hope to Nineveh, doomed though it was, of a merciful respite on its repentance. The patience and pity of God stand in striking contrast with the selfishness and hard-heartedness of man.<div eID="gen23429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23430" type="x-p"/> Nineveh in particular was chosen to teach Israel these lessons, on account of its being capital of the then world kingdom, and because it was now beginning to make its power felt by Israel. Our Lord (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.41">Mt 12:41</reference>) makes Nineveh's repentance a reproof of the Jews' impenitence in His day, just as Jonah provoked Israel to jealousy (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">De 32:21</reference>) by the same example. Jonah's mission to Nineveh implied that a heathen city afforded as legitimate a field for the prophet's labors as Israel, and with a more successful result (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Am 9:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23431" type="x-p"/> The book is prose narrative throughout, except the prayer of thanksgiving in the second chapter (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.1-Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:1-9</reference>). The Chaldæisms in the original do not prove spuriousness, or a later age, but were natural in the language of one living in Zebulun on the borders of the north, whence Aramaic peculiarities would readily arise; moreover, his message to Nineveh implies acquaintance with Assyrian. Living as Jonah did in a part of Israel exposed to Assyrian invasions, he probably stood in the same relation to Assyria as Elijah and Elisha had stood to Syria. The purity of the language implies the antiquity of the book, and the likelihood of its being Jonah's own writing. Indeed, none but Jonah could have written or dictated such peculiar details, known only to himself.<div eID="gen23431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23432" type="x-p"/> The tradition that places the tomb of Jonah opposite to Mosul, and names it "Nebbi Junus" (that is, "prophet Jonah"), originated probably in the spot having been occupied by a Christian church or convent dedicated to him [Layard]. A more ancient tradition of Jerome's time placed the tomb in Jonah's native village of Gath-hepher.<div eID="gen23432" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jonah.1.1-Jonah.1.17">Jon 1:1-17</reference>. Jonah's Commission to Nineveh, Flight, Punishment, and Preservation by Miracle.</title> <div sID="gen23433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12669"/><hi type="bold">1. Jonah--</hi>meaning in Hebrew, "dove." Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.8.8">Ge 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.9">9</reference>, where the dove in vain seeks rest after flying from Noah and the ark: so Jonah. Grotius not so well explains it, "one sprung from Greece" or Ionia, where there were prophets called Amythaonidæ.<div eID="gen23433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23434" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Amittai--</hi>Hebrew for "truth," "truth-telling"; appropriate to a prophet. <div eID="gen23434" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5cd766c6460800911831be8a855f317bd2e1573: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12670"/><div sID="gen23435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12670"/><hi type="bold">2. to Nineveh--</hi>east of the Tigris, opposite the modern Mosul. The only case of a prophet being sent to the heathen. Jonah, however, is sent to Nineveh, not solely for Nineveh's good, but also to shame Israel, by the fact of a heathen city repenting at the first preaching of a single stranger, Jonah, whereas God's people will not repent, though preached to by their many national prophets, late and early. Nineveh means "the residence of Ninus," that is, Nimrod. <reference osisRef="Gen.10.11">Ge 10:11</reference>, where the translation ought to be, "He (Nimrod) went forth into Assyria and builded Nineveh." Modern research into the cuneiform inscriptions confirms the Scripture account that Babylon was founded earlier than Nineveh, and that both cities were built by descendants of Ham, encroaching on the territory assigned to Shem (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Ge 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.8">6, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.25">10, 25</reference>).<div eID="gen23435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great city--</hi>four hundred eighty stadia in circumference, one hundred fifty in length, and ninety in breadth [Diodorus Siculus, 2.3]. Taken by Arbaces the Mede, in the reign of Sardanapalus, about the seventh year of Uzziah; and a second time by Nabopolassar of Babylon and Cyaxares the Mede in 625 B.C. See on <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.3">Jon 3:3</reference>.<div eID="gen23436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Is 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">58:1</reference>).<div eID="gen23437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come up before me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Ge 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.6.13">6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.6">Ezr 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.5">Re 18:5</reference>); that is, their wickedness is so great as to require My open interposition for punishment. <div eID="gen23438" type="x-p"/>
entries.a50abe227ee150a320f54aabdffd40786f9ac74f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12671"/><div sID="gen23439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12671"/><hi type="bold">3. flee--</hi>Jonah's motive for flight is hinted at in <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.2">Jon 4:2</reference>: fear that after venturing on such a dangerous commission to so powerful a heathen city, his prophetical threats should be set aside by God's "repenting of the evil," just as God had so long spared Israel notwithstanding so many provocations, and so he should seem a false prophet. Besides, he may have felt it beneath him to discharge a commission to a foreign idolatrous nation, whose destruction he desired rather than their repentance. This is the only case of a prophet, charged with a prophetical message, concealing it.<div eID="gen23439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the presence of the Lord--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.4.16">Ge 4:16</reference>). Jonah thought in fleeing from the land of Israel, where Jehovah was peculiarly present, that he should escape from Jehovah's prophecy-inspiring influence. He probably knew the truth stated in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.7-Ps.139.10">Psa 139:7-10</reference>, but virtually ignored it (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.3.8-Gen.3.10">Ge 3:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.24">Jr 23:24</reference>).<div eID="gen23440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23441" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went down--</hi>appropriate in going from land to the sea (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.23">Psa 107:23</reference>).<div eID="gen23441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joppa--</hi>now Jaffa, in the region of Dan; a harbor as early as Solomon's time (<reference osisRef="2Chr.2.16">2Ch 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tarshish--</hi>Tartessus in Spain; in the farthest west at the greatest distance from Nineveh in the east. <div eID="gen23443" type="x-p"/>
entries.49d56569a89a36d273a498c9c5ac5ef845ca8838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12672"/><div sID="gen23444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12672"/><hi type="bold">4. sent out--</hi>literally, caused a wind to burst forth. Coverdale translates, "hurled a greate wynde into the see." <div eID="gen23444" type="x-p"/>
entries.98048001bfe6fe9e1a42c0e4e02ed2a810e3fc70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12673"/><div sID="gen23445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12673"/><hi type="bold">5. mariners were afraid--</hi>though used to storms; the danger therefore must have been extreme.<div eID="gen23445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cried every man unto his god--</hi>The idols proved unable to save them, though each, according to Phoenician custom, called on his tutelary god. But Jehovah proved able: and the heathen sailors owned it in the end by sacrificing to Him (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.16">Jon 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen23446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the sides--</hi>that is, the interior recesses (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3">1Sa 24:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.15">15</reference>). Those conscious of guilt shrink from the presence of their fellow man into concealment.<div eID="gen23447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fast asleep--</hi>Sleep is no necessary proof of innocence; it may be the fruit of carnal security and a seared conscience. How different was Jesus' sleep on the Sea of Galilee! (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.37-Mark.4.39">Mr 4:37-39</reference>). Guilty Jonah's indifference to fear contrasts with the unoffending mariners' alarm. The original therefore is in the nominative absolute: "But as for Jonah, he," &c. Compare spiritually, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>. <div eID="gen23448" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce6003210f35fadd69663b823f1b4389b3ee3519: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12674"/><div sID="gen23449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12674"/><hi type="bold">6. call upon thy God--</hi>The ancient heathen in dangers called on foreign gods, besides their national ones (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.107.28">Psa 107:28</reference>). Maurer translates the preceding clause, "What is the reason that thou sleepest?"<div eID="gen23449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think upon us--</hi>for good (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.8.1">Ge 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.2.25">Ex 2:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.17">Psa 40:17</reference>). <div eID="gen23450" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5dbea5dc90f69c874bcf221a605c06e052f02eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12675"/><div sID="gen23451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12675"/><hi type="bold">7. cast lots--</hi>God sometimes sanctioned this mode of deciding in difficult cases. Compare the similar instance of Achan, whose guilt involved Israel in suffering, until God revealed the offender, probably by the casting of lots (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.33">Pr 16:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.26">Ac 1:26</reference>). Primitive tradition and natural conscience led even the heathen to believe that one guilty man involves all his associates, though innocent, in punishment. So Cicero [The Nature of the Gods, 3.37] mentions that the mariners sailing with Diagoras, an atheist, attributed a storm that overtook them to his presence in the ship (compare Horace's Odes, 3.2.26). <div eID="gen23451" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5ec18f6726937d61dc30785ac318a3089134657: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12676"/><div sID="gen23452" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12676"/>8. The guilty individual being discovered is interrogated so as to make full confession with his own mouth. So in Achan's case (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.19">Jos 7:19</reference>). <div eID="gen23452" type="x-p"/>
entries.3155c43729326021e511c82325a5e2cfed673902: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12677"/><div sID="gen23453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12677"/><hi type="bold">9. I am an Hebrew--</hi>He does not say "an Israelite." For this was the name used among themselves; "Hebrew," among foreigners (<reference osisRef="Gen.40.15">Ge 40:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.3.18">Ex 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen23453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I fear the Lord--</hi>in profession: his practice belied his profession: his profession aggravated his guilt.<div eID="gen23454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God ... which ... made the sea--</hi>appropriately expressed, as accounting for the tempest sent on the sea. The heathen had distinct gods for the "heaven," the "sea," and the "land." Jehovah is the one and only true God of all alike. Jonah at last is awakened by the violent remedy from his lethargy. Jonah was but the reflection of Israel's backsliding from God, and so must bear the righteous punishment. The guilt of the minister is the result of that of the people, as in Moses' case (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.21">De 4:21</reference>). This is what makes Jonah a suitable type of Messiah, who bore the imputed sin of the people. <div eID="gen23455" type="x-p"/>
entries.a08240e26fcd1be07453f0a8c24950c499b884a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12678"/><div sID="gen23456" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12678"/>10. "The men were exceedingly afraid," when made aware of the wrath of so powerful a God at the flight of Jonah.<div eID="gen23456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Why hast thou done this?--</hi>If professors of religion do wrong, they will hear of it from those who make no such profession. <div eID="gen23457" type="x-p"/>
entries.b472f9b3a1f7a5eff951c54769ec88ff98ef050c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12679"/><div sID="gen23458" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12679"/><hi type="bold">11. What shall we do unto thee?--</hi>They ask this, as Jonah himself must best know how his God is to be appeased. "We would gladly save thee, if we can do so, and yet be saved ourselves" (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.13">Jon 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen23458" type="x-p"/>
entries.023a126d77e1be5810aac36bce5e50b4281ccaf2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12680"/><div sID="gen23459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12680"/><hi type="bold">12. cast me ... into the sea--</hi>Herein Jonah is a type of Messiah, the one man who offered Himself to die, in order to allay the stormy flood of God's wrath (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.69.1">Psa 69:1</reference>, 2, as to Messiah), which otherwise must have engulfed all other men. So Caiaphas by the Spirit declared it expedient that one man should die, and that the whole nation should not perish (<reference osisRef="John.11.50">Joh 11:50</reference>). Jonah also herein is a specimen of true repentance, which leads the penitent to "accept the punishment of his iniquity" (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">Le 26:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.43">43</reference>), and to be more indignant at his sin than at his suffering. <div eID="gen23459" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4d93d5bce130a3004b732447d1a70bdb491a619: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12681"/><div sID="gen23460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12681"/><hi type="bold">13. they could not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.21.30">Pr 21:30</reference>). Wind and tide--God's displeasure and God's counsel--were against them. <div eID="gen23460" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4d42631dbef7dc3e4a4c1f4534f2bc1994b40f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12682"/><div sID="gen23461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12682"/><hi type="bold">14. for this man's life--</hi>that is, for taking this man's life.<div eID="gen23461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">innocent blood--</hi>Do not punish us as Thou wouldst punish the shedders of innocent blood (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.21.8">De 21:8</reference>). In the case of the Antitype, Pontius Pilate washed his hands and confessed Christ's innocence, "I am innocent of the blood of this just person." But whereas Jonah the victim was guilty and the sailors innocent, Christ our sacrificial victim was innocent and Pontius Pilate and nil of us men were guilty.
