               <ns0:p n="4">4 ¶ But the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Almighty and Eternal God from whose work <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> flieth.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>cast forth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sent out <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">God keepeth the winds as in Store-houses, or trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suries, and now brings one forth to fetch back a Fugitive, and obstinate refuser of his Command,</ns0:note> a great wind <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">the greatness of it, with the suddenness of its rising, and manner of its working, undeni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ably shew'd that 'twas supernatural<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and from God displeased with all, or with some one or other of them.</ns0:note> into the sea <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The winds did not blow aloft over the sea and ship, but as if they had intermixt with the very waters of the Sea, and like an unheard of Hurricane shaked the very keel of the ship;</ns0:note>, and there was a mighty tempest in the sea <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That part of the Sea where <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi>'s ship was, this Messenger soon finds out <ns0:hi>Ionah,</ns0:hi> and speaks in most dreadful manner to all in the ship, who all saw and own<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed it to be from Heaven, the finger of God.</ns0:note>, so that the ship <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>thought to be broken.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> was like to be broken <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Master, and Mariners thought they, Ship, and Goods, and all should be lost; the <ns0:hi>Hebr.</ns0:hi> expresseth it as if the Ship had sense of God's anger, as if the ship could think, and did think of its own weakness, and God's mighty hand.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Then <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">When this praeternatural Tempest fell with all its violence into the Sea,</ns0:note> the mariners <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Passengers are not here named, who unaccusto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med to Sea, might be too apprehensive of danger, but the men that were acquainted with the Sea, and had seen many a Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pest, and weathered many a storm,</ns0:note> were afraid <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">heartily afraid, full of apprehensions that they should be wrack't.</ns0:note>, and cryed <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">With loud voice and earnest petitions, as the manner of such men is, when danger awakens them to the Duty they neglect whilest safe.</ns0:note> every man <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Not a man of them but feared, nor a man of them but cryed out, by which it is evident it twas a most dreadful storm.</ns0:note> unto his god <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By this it appears that the ships crue was a mixture of men who worshipt several Gods, and every one doth now cry to the God whom he Worshipt, what ever God it might be, 'twas not he that did raise, nor could allay the Tempest.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">So Act 27.18, 19.</ns0:note> cast forth the wares that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> in the ship <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">When Prayer to their false Gods doth no good, but their danger continued and threat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned them with foundring in the Sea; to prevent this, they lighten the ship, as is usual in such cases, and cast the Wares out; not as Sacrifice to the God of the Sea, or as repenting of Piracy by which the Goods were gotten, though some conje<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cture so, but the Text tells us 'twas to lighten the Ship,</ns0:note> into the sea to lighten <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> of them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">that it may bear up its head, and work with the Sea better than when heavy laden.</ns0:note>, But Jonah <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The greatest weight, and only danger to Ship and Sea-men</ns0:note> was gon down into the sides of the ship <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">was under the hold in some Cabin or other in the side of the Ship, whither he went before the storm arose</ns0:note>, and he lay, and was fast asleep <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">in a very deep sleep, as the word imports.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:175" />6 So the ship-master <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Who had the conduct of the Vessel, and from whose mouth such a reproof was seasonable,</ns0:note> came to him <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">missing him, when all the rest were toil'd with labour, and had been crying mightily to their false Gods, but <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> appeared not.</ns0:note>, and said unto him, What meanest thou, O * sleeper <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">A very decent yet sharp reproof to him, What mettal art thou made of? Or, What God dost thou fear? Or, Art thou deaf to all the mena<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces of Heaven?</ns0:note>! arise <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Awake, get up,</ns0:note>, call upon thy God <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Pray to that God thou worshippest, as we have already each done, for possibly thy God may be mightier than our Gods, and may lay the Tempest that lyeth so heavily upon us.</ns0:note>, if so be that God <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">They had lost the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>r labour seeking to other Gods, yet think it adviseable, that <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> should try his God too, if so be, <ns0:hi>&c. Vid. Ioel</ns0:hi> 2.14. and so <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 5.15.</ns0:note> will think upon us <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">With pitty, care, and favour, and do for us in this our strange distress,</ns0:note>, that we perish not <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">that Ship, Goods, and Men too, may not be lost.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 And they said every one to his fellow <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">After they had prayed, which was necessary in such cases, as being a religious means, and cast out the Goods which load<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the Ship, which was a proper natural means of safety, but none appeared, still the Tempest, and their Danger with it con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinued, a shrew'd Symptom that there was one or other amongst them whose sins had provoked God to do this, and that 'twere fit to be known who this was, and who e're first moved for mak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the search, all agree in the expedient.</ns0:note>, Come <ns0:note n="†" place="bottom">'Tis like that it was upon the thoughts of many of them, and so exprest here.</ns0:note> and let us cast lots <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It is extraordinary danger we are in, all ordinary means fail, let us try that which hath somewhat extraordinary in it, though many times used, let the lot decide among us who is the cause of all this; lots are an appeal to Heaven in doubtful cases, and therefore not to be used on trifling, or unnecessary cases, but where the matter is great, difficult, or undeterminable in any other way, as Scripture instances of lots do inform us. <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 16.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 26.55. <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 14.2. and 18.6. and 21. 4, 5, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 10.20. &c. <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 10.34. and 11.1. <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> chosen by lot, and <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 1.26.</ns0:note>, that we may know for whose cause this evil <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Very great, unusual, and praeternatural Tempest, not one among them but had de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served more, yet they surmise some notorious offender amongst them, or this had not been.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon us: So they cast lots <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">They act according to what was proposed.</ns0:note>, and the lot fell upon Jonah <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">God determins and singles out <ns0:hi>Ionah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Then said they unto him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">When the lot pointed out <ns0:hi>Ionah,</ns0:hi> these Marriners all are satisfied that he was the man; that Heaven had determined that grand Enquiry, and accordingly they treat with him.</ns0:note>, Tell us we pray thee <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">They do try what fair means will do with him, and desire to have the account from his own mouth; so <ns0:hi>Ioshua</ns0:hi> dealt with <ns0:hi>Achan, Iosh.</ns0:hi> 7. satisfied in the person, next they do with commenda<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble justice, and calmness enquire into the thing.</ns0:note>, for whose cause this evil <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon us <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">What hast thou done, for which God is so angry with thee, and with us for thy sake; sure thou canst not but know what 'tis, and now frankly tell us</ns0:note>? what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thine occupation <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">what course of Life hast thou lived, or what Imployment dost thou now profess to follow, that we may guess by that whether thou art one of flagitious, or of honest Life?</ns0:note>? and whence comest thou <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">E're he give answer to this, probably another asketh whence he cometh, what Company he had kept; by this they conje<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cture at the man.</ns0:note>? what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy countrey <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Another starts a third Enquiry, what Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />try or Nation he is of, to those Ports Persons of different Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions flockt, possibly they hoped some or other in the ship might be his Country-men, and so fittest to e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>amin him.</ns0:note>, and of what people <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> thou <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">This seems to be the same question repeated, or else an En<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quiry where he dwelt. These the heads of the Questions askt him.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And he said unto them <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> freely and readily gives account of himself.</ns0:note> I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> an Hebrew <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">One that am descended from <ns0:hi>Heber,</ns0:hi> whose Off-spring by <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> are well known, and probably to these Mariners, he saith not a <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> because he was not in strictness of speech, for he was of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Zebulun,</ns0:hi> nor an <ns0:hi>Israelite</ns0:hi> distinguisht from the <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> lest he should seem to own himself of that Idolatrous Faction.</ns0:note>, and I fear <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">I worship and serve the true God only, or possibly it may imply that his employment was in the immediate service of God, as a Religious person that had abdicated the World, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dicated himself to God.</ns0:note> the LORD <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The Eternal, and Almighty God, yours are upstart Gods, and have no power or might, nor can they do any thing.</ns0:note> the God of heaven <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who first made, now ruleth, and ever will rule the Heavens which none of your Gods can pretend to, those Heavens from whence you see this storm falleth.</ns0:note>, which hath made the sea <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That Sea which now threatens you for my sake, and threatens me for my sin, my God hath raised the Sea in his quarrel to contend thus furiously, and he can, and none but he can command it to be still.</ns0:note>, and the dry land <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">A Description of the Earth, you would get thither, but all your Gods cannot bring you thither, or give you to set one foot upon it if my God say no. This is the sum of what <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> declares, by which he intimateth his innocency from any flagitious Crime as they might imagin him guilty, and yet confesseth the greatness of his sin which he had before told them, though they understood it not, or thought light of it, he fled from the presence of the Lord.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Then <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">When <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> had declared his God, whose power and wrath these Mariners saw and heard in the Tempest, and what sin of his was now punisht, and how they had taken him into their ship, knowing that he did run away from this mighty God.</ns0:note> were the men <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                        <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> exceedingly a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fraid <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Their fear was doubled, every thing now represents horrour to them, their own danger, <ns0:hi>Nineveh</ns0:hi>'s approaching dismal ruin which they believe by what they see; satisfied, that he so tremendously punisht the refusal to deliver the message, was able, and certainly would execute the sentence which he commanded should be delivered.</ns0:note>, and said unto him, Why hast thou done <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Now they ask a reason for that of which no reason can be given; It was most unreasonable that <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> had done, and we find no answer to this interrogatory, though the foregoing questions were answered; others think 'tis a re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proof of him for so doing, I rather think it mixt of both; 'twas a real reproof to him-self while he more particularly explains the great sinfulness of this prank of his; and 'tis an enquiry made for satisfaction to them, who no doubt thought of <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nah</ns0:hi>'s God as they did of their own, that 'twas no hard mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter to be done, nor any great sin, if done, to run from their presence. These likely were their thoughts of the thing when he first told them; but the dreadful storm that <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi>'s God sent after this fugitive Servant of his, makes them more curious to know what great sin it was, and so <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> explaining the whole, confesseth his sin, humbleth himself, and takes the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proof to himself, and informeth them aright.</ns0:note> this? for the men <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Master of the Ship, and the Marriners.</ns0:note> knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In these words 'tis probable he told them, now though they knew this was the thing yet they apprehended not what was in it, but did judge of this by their own Gods, and their presence,</ns0:note>, because he had told <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">when they enquired the cause of his Travels, as 'tis very like they would do, e're they took his fare.</ns0:note> them</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 ¶ Then <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">When they heard all that <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> had declared to them, and well weigh'd it all, and saw it lookt, all of one piece, most credible.</ns0:note> said they unto him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">A Prophet fittest in that respect to tell them what should be done, and a Party so highly concerned in it.</ns0:note>, What shall we do unto thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">If thy God will by thee declare his Will, and we do it, we shall not provoke him, and if thou submit to his Will, and direct us, we shall not injure thee.</ns0:note> that the sea <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">

                  </ns0:note> wrought and was tempestuous <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Though <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> had recounted all, and given Glory to God, taken shame to himself, and satisfied the Sea-men, yet the Sea grew higher and higher, more tempestuous in it self, and more dangerous to them, and they were sensible that somewhat must be done with <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> to quiet all. Their fear was lest they should mistake herein, and therefore they ask his Counsel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And he said unto them <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He readily gives them advice for their safety.</ns0:note>, Take me up <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This he spake as a Prophet directed of God, and not as some <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Rabbi thinks choosing to die rather than to go to <ns0:hi>Nineveh.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and cast me forth into the sea <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Throw me overboard into the Sea, no other way must you deal with me than this, and this way I not only direct as expe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dient, but from God I give you it as a Command, and you must do it, thus my God-will punish my disobedience and contempt.</ns0:note>, so shall the sea be calm unto you <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">As a Prophet I assure you the Tempest shall cease, and you be safe, and by that you may know I being in the ship, endanger'd you all.</ns0:note>, for I know <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">I am assured of this, and though I have been your danger, and this was my fault, yet it shall not be my fault if you be drowned.</ns0:note> that for my sake <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For my sin which God will punish, but not by my own act, I must not leap over board, 'tis a crime God will punish by that Justice which is in this place,</ns0:note> this great tempest <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon you <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">and will be till you have executed God's sentence on me, which I willingly submit to.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:175" />13 Nevertheless <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>And, Heb.</ns0:hi> but rightly to the proper sense of the phrase rendred here <ns0:hi>nevertheless,</ns0:hi> not withstanding the lot fell on <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nah,</ns0:hi> he confessed his fault, directs them to cast him over board, and in all this avoweth himself to be a Prophet of God, and as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sures them of a calm Sea if they do this, yet very willing to save him.</ns0:note> the men <ns0:note place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>digged.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> rowed hard <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">They contrived all wayes, and are willing to be at any labour to save him; they ply their oars, and strain their strength with deep stroaks to force the Ship to shoar.</ns0:note> to bring <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to land, but they could <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">All was lost labour, God had given other order to his Servants, the Wind and Sea, both obey him, and both keep <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> a Prisoner, self condemned, and desirous of what the Marriners were very unwilling to.</ns0:note> not; for the sea wrought, and was tempestuous against them <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Vid, ver.</ns0:hi> 11. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> i. the Sea tost it self more violently, and by unsteddy motions like some Hurricane every moment endangered them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Wherefore <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Since all their labour and skill to carry the ship to shore<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> was successless, and they saw no remedy, but they must either follow <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi>'s advice against himself, or drown with him.</ns0:note> they cryed <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">With importunity of mind, and with loud voices too in prayer.</ns0:note> unto the LORD <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Not now as in beginning of the Tempest every man to his God, but better instructed now they all do cry to <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi>'s God, to <ns0:hi>Iehovah</ns0:hi> the true God.</ns0:note>, and said, We <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">They all join in Prayer,</ns0:note> beseech <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">sue to Mercy for Mercy, they plead not innocency, or merit, but pray for mercy, and that free.</ns0:note> thee <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">All sue to God, not to Saints, or intermediate <ns0:hi>Daemons.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, O LORD, we beseech thee <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">'Tis repeated to note their vehe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mency in prayer,</ns0:note>, let us not perish for this mans life <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Though he is pointed out by lot, hath ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vised us hereunto, yet if possible let the tempest cease, and we all be safe, let not him perish, nor we for him, so their first Prayer is for safety to <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> and all in the Ship.</ns0:note>, and lay not upon us innocent blood <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This the next suit that if God by the continued Tempest do perempto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rily and irreversibly require <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi>'s Life, a person innocent a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mong them, and had, since he came to them so demean'd him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, so that should they throw him overboard, before they had tryed all kind of means for preserving him, they might be just<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly accounted barbarous Murtherers, and God would certainly charge innocent blood upon them; This they deprecate with all earnestness and importunity.</ns0:note>: for thou, O LORD, hast done <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Sending the Tempest, ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />resting the Prophet by it, detecting him by lot, sentencing him by his own mouth, and confirming the condemning sentence by the continuance of the storm, and so leaving us to perish with this offender against thee, or to be thy Executioners, this is thine own doing, and 'tis just because thou doest it:</ns0:note> as it pleased thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Though it be secret to us, and strange in our opinion, yet 'tis very just and necessary we know, or it would not please thee it should be so.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 So <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>And, Heb.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> they took up Jonah <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">As he advised with regret to themselves, though with full consent of <ns0:hi>Jonah,</ns0:hi> at last they yield.</ns0:note>, and cast him forth into the sea <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">

                  </ns0:note> ceased from her raging <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">As <ns0:hi>Jonah</ns0:hi> had assured them, so they find the Sea all on a sudden calm and friendly, which we must under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand includes the wind sent into the Sea, though it be not mentioned here.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Then <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">When they saw God approved the thing, and confirmed <ns0:hi>Jonah</ns0:hi>'s word, as of a true Prophet, and had spared them.</ns0:note> the men <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The Sea-men, and all others, if any others were in the ship</ns0:note> feared the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">With a deep reverence of his Power, Wisdom, and Justice against <ns0:hi>Jonah,</ns0:hi> and of his Mercy towards them. What was the final effect of this, and whether they were by it throughly turned to God, I enquire not now, it may best become our charity that as <ns0:hi>Jonah</ns0:hi>'s casting overboard was Type of Christ's Death, so the effect it had upon the Mariners might be a Type of the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />version of the Heathen from Idols to God.</ns0:note> ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceedingly <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Their fear before was exceeding great, but that was a fear of the danger, and for themselves a natural fear; but now they do fear the Lord and his Majesty and Mercy, it is a Religious fear.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note place="margin">

                  </ns0:note> made vows <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Vows are a part of Natural Religion, and here these persons bind them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves by vows to recognise God's goodness in their delive<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance. It is not improbable that here is a Trajection as many times in Scripture, that placed last which in construction is to be first. They vowed Vows and Sacrificed, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> vowed they would do it, would be Proselytes, and ever Worship him, <ns0:hi>Jo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nah</ns0:hi> preacht to them, Creator of Heaven and Earth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
